source.name: UZH Methodenberatung, section 'Datenanalyse mit SPSS': methods taxonomy pages, overview decision graphic and step-wise decision assistant

components.description: 34 HTML pages under /de/datenanalyse_spss(.html|/...): overview, 11 branch/intermediate pages, 22 method (leaf) pages
static image map + JPEG (entscheidbaum.html/.jpg), iframe on the overview page

source.use_policy: External methodological background and provenance only. Executable guidance in inferguidR is R-only, with no SPSS syntax or workflow. All labels, questions and descriptions here are original paraphrases or short labels; no source prose or graphics are reproduced.

retrieval.tools: Python 3.14.4 with requests 2.32.5 and beautifulsoup4 4.14.3; curl. Single pass with 0.5-1 s delay between requests; scope restricted to /de/datenanalyse_spss and /static/entscheidbaum|entscheidassistent.

nodes.question_en: Is there prior theory and a concrete question about how designated outcome and explanatory variables relate (dependence analysis), or is structure among many variables/objects to be discovered (interdependence analysis)? The overview page additionally lists univariate description.
nodes.question_de: Konkrete Fragestellung prüfen oder Strukturen entdecken? (zusätzlich: univariate Beschreibung)

source_refs.locator: sub-page list of the overview page

condition_soundness.note_en: The assistant equates 'theory exists' with dependence analysis and 'discover structure' with interdependence analysis. Confirmatory versus exploratory intent is a separate axis: regression can be exploratory, and factor analysis can be confirmatory (the interdependence page itself mentions confirmatory factor analysis). inferguidR should ask for the aim/estimand explicitly instead of inferring it from how much theory exists.

notes: Root of the overview graphic and first assistant page. The descriptive branch is attested only by the overview page's sub-page navigation, not by the graphic or the assistant.

nodes.condition: Aim is to describe single variables (frequencies, location, spread, shape) before or instead of inferential analysis.
nodes.description_en: Describes variables one at a time with frequency tables and graphics, location and dispersion measures, and shape measures. Stated purposes: data-entry checks, spotting outliers, and judging whether data suit later procedures.
nodes.description_de: Beschreibung einzelner Variablen: Häufigkeiten, Lage, Streuung, Form.

source_rules.source_says_en: Approximate normality is called the most important precondition of many procedures. Data must be checked for normality beforehand, e.g. with a chi-square goodness-of-fit test, and a procedure without a normality requirement must be used if the violation is too strong.
source_rules.correction_en: Do not implement 'normality test significant -> switch to rank test' as a universal rule. Normality pre-tests have size and power problems: they are insensitive in small samples, where it matters, and over-sensitive in large samples, where it rarely matters. Conditioning the main test on a pre-test also distorts its error rates. The relevant distribution is usually that of residuals or paired differences, not the raw pooled data. Rank tests change the estimand. Choose the method from design, estimand, sample size and robustness instead.

source_rules.source_says_en: Standardising (z-transformation) is described as necessary when procedures require normally distributed data.
source_rules.correction_en: A z-transformation is linear and leaves the shape of a distribution unchanged. It cannot make data normal and is not a remedy for non-normality.

source_rules.source_says_en: Rule of thumb: in a left-skewed distribution mean < median < mode, and in a right-skewed one the reverse.
source_rules.correction_en: This textbook rule fails often, particularly for discrete or multimodal distributions. Treat it as illustrative only.

source_rules.source_says_en: The kurtosis of a normal distribution is stated as 0.
source_rules.correction_en: This holds for excess kurtosis; the raw fourth standardised moment of a normal distribution is 3. State which definition is used.

condition_soundness.note_en: Description as a separate aim is appropriate.

notes: Not part of the overview graphic or the assistant; reached only from the overview page navigation.

nodes.condition: Prior theory or a concrete research question exists; variables are designated in advance as dependent (to be explained) or independent (explanatory).
nodes.description_en: Hypothesis-testing procedures that examine how designated dependent variables depend on independent variables, subdivided into differences and associations. Introduces the null/alternative hypotheses, significance level, and type I/II errors.
nodes.description_de: Strukturprüfende Verfahren mit abhängigen und unabhängigen Variablen.

source_rules.source_says_en: With alpha = 5%, p < .05 is said to mean a probability above 95% that the variance in the data did not arise by chance.
source_rules.correction_en: A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed, computed assuming the null model is true. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis, or 'chance', is true or false.

source_rules.source_says_en: The significance level is said to depend, among other things, on sample size and population size.
source_rules.correction_en: Alpha is a design choice fixed before analysis, not a quantity that depends on sample or population size. Its choice can be justified by the consequences of errors, and power depends on n.

source_rules.source_says_en: Describes deciding to 'accept' a hypothesis.
source_rules.correction_en: A non-significant result does not establish the null hypothesis. Report an estimate with a confidence interval, and use equivalence testing if absence of a relevant effect is the claim.

notes: Image-map area for 'Dependenzanalyse' in entscheidbaum.html has a malformed href (a space inside the host name), so the link is dead; see gap uzh.gap.broken_imagemap_dependenz.

In the URL hierarchy 'unterschiede' and 'zusammenhaenge' are siblings of 'dependenz'; they are placed under dependence here because the graphic, sub-graphic, page text and assistant all group them that way.

nodes.condition: Next decision within dependence analysis.
nodes.question_en: Should associations between variables be examined, or differences (between groups or measurements)?

condition_soundness.note_en: This is a pedagogical split, not a statistical one: a two-group mean difference is also an association between a binary predictor and the outcome (regression with a dummy variable). Proportion comparisons between groups sit under 'associations' (contingency chi-square), not under 'differences'.

nodes.condition: The question concerns the association (relationship) between variables.
nodes.description_en: Six procedures: four for two variables (Pearson correlation, simple regression, Spearman rank correlation, Pearson chi-square contingency analysis) and two for several predictors with one outcome (multiple and logistic regression). Extensions for nominal and ordinal outcomes are mentioned without a page of their own.
nodes.description_de: Sechs Verfahren für Zusammenhänge zwischen zwei bzw. mehreren Variablen.
notes: Mentioned without a leaf: regression extensions for nominal (multinomial) and ordinal outcomes.

nodes.condition: Next decision within associations.
nodes.question_en: Is the association between exactly two variables of interest, or between more than two (several predictors, one outcome)?

condition_soundness.note_en: Counting variables is a proxy. The real distinction is one predictor versus several (adjusted) predictors, and the outcome's type determines the model family, whatever the count.

nodes.label_en: Scale level of the two variables?
nodes.condition: Exactly two variables.
nodes.question_en: Are both variables interval-scaled, ordinal, or nominal?

condition_soundness.note_en: This assumes both variables share one scale level. Mixed pairs, such as binary with interval or nominal with ordinal, are not routed; a binary-interval pair is a two-group comparison or point-biserial correlation. Scale level should be confirmed from what the variables mean, not from how they are stored. The 'scale levels' info link on this assistant page returns HTTP 404 (gap uzh.gap.assistant_scale_link_404).

nodes.label_en: Is one variable designated as dependent?
nodes.condition: Both variables interval-scaled.
nodes.question_en: Is one variable assumed to depend on the other (a presumed causal direction), or is an undirected association assumed with no variable designated as dependent?

condition_soundness.note_en: The source chooses regression over correlation by presumed causal direction. The choice should instead follow the estimand: the conditional mean or prediction of Y given X (regression) versus a symmetric measure of linear association (correlation). Neither method can show causation. With two random variables the test of slope = 0 equals the test of rho = 0. inferguidR must not recommend a causal reading from a significant coefficient.

nodes.condition: Two interval variables; one designated as dependent (directed hypothesis).
nodes.description_en: Tests and describes a linear relationship between one predictor and one outcome. Page covers assumption checks: residual plots, Breusch-Pagan/White tests, Durbin-Watson, a residual histogram, and robust standard errors as a remedy for heteroscedasticity.
nodes.description_de: Linearer Zusammenhang einer unabhängigen mit einer abhängigen Variable.

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: Regression is introduced as cause analysis ('Ursachenanalyse'), with the caveat that any postulated causal relationship must be justified by theory.
source_rules.correction_en: Regression estimates conditional associations. A causal interpretation requires design-based or explicit causal assumptions, which inferguidR must elicit rather than infer from significance.

source_rules.source_says_en: The predictor is required to be interval-scaled.
source_rules.correction_en: Predictors may be binary or dummy-coded categorical (the multiple-regression page itself allows dummies). Only the error-distribution assumptions concern the outcome.

condition_soundness.note_en: The routing relies on presumed causal direction; see uzh.q.assoc.two.interval.direction. The stated assumptions correctly target residuals.

nodes.condition: Two interval variables; no variable designated as dependent (undirected association).
nodes.description_en: Quantifies the strength and direction of a linear association between two interval variables without implying a direction; r doubles as an effect size.
nodes.description_de: Linearer, ungerichteter Zusammenhang zweier intervallskalierter Variablen.

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: Both variables are required to be normally distributed.
source_rules.correction_en: As a descriptive measure of linear association, r needs no normality. The usual t-test and Fisher-z interval are exact under bivariate normality, which marginal normality does not guarantee, and approximately valid for moderate n. Outliers and non-linearity matter more than marginal shape. Permutation or bootstrap inference is an alternative.

condition_soundness.note_en: Routing by presumed causal direction; see uzh.q.assoc.two.interval.direction.

nodes.condition: Two ordinal variables.
nodes.description_en: Rank-based association between two (at least) ordinal variables, presented as the non-parametric counterpart of Pearson correlation and usable with small samples and outliers.

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: Spearman's coefficient is described as measuring the linear association of two ordinal variables.
source_rules.correction_en: Spearman's rho measures monotonic association; it is the Pearson correlation of the ranks, so it is 'linear' only on the rank scale. Ties require mid-ranks, and with many ties Kendall's tau-b is an alternative.

source_rules.source_says_en: Used when the parametric correlation's preconditions are not met.
source_rules.correction_en: Switching changes the estimand from linear to monotonic association. Choose by the question asked, not by a failed pre-test.

condition_soundness.note_en: Ordinal-ordinal pairs are appropriately routed. Interval data with outliers or monotonic non-linearity can also justify Spearman, which the assistant does not route.

nodes.label_en: Pearson chi-square test of independence (contingency analysis)
nodes.condition: Two nominal variables (the page says nominal or ordinal, i.e. categorical).
method_names: Yates continuity correction (as stated by source)
Fisher exact test (as stated by source)
nodes.description_en: Cross-tabulates two categorical variables and compares observed with expected counts under independence, then reports association strength (phi, Cramér's V, contingency coefficient).
nodes.description_de: Zusammenhang zweier kategorialer Variablen in einer Kreuztabelle.
source_preconditions_en: n > 50; Fisher's test if n < 20, Yates correction if 20-50
all expected counts > 5, otherwise Fisher's test

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: Fisher's exact test is said to be based on simulations and to have no assumptions.
source_rules.correction_en: Fisher's test conditions on both margins and uses the hypergeometric distribution by exact enumeration; Monte Carlo is only an optional approximation for large tables. It assumes independent observations and makes inference conditional on the margins. That makes it conservative when only one margin is fixed by design, as in two independent binomial samples.

source_rules.source_says_en: Fisher's test if n < 20; Yates correction if 20 <= n <= 50; uncorrected chi-square only if n > 50.
source_rules.correction_en: These thresholds are not standard criteria. For 2x2 tables Campbell (2007) recommends the 'N-1' chi-square when all expected counts are >= 1 and the Fisher-Irwin test otherwise. For two independent proportions, unconditional exact tests (Boschloo, Barnard) are more powerful than Fisher's test, and Boschloo's test is uniformly more powerful than it.

source_rules.source_says_en: With df = 1 the Yates correction is recommended.
source_rules.correction_en: The Yates correction is overly conservative and not recommended as a routine default.

source_rules.source_says_en: All expected cell counts must exceed 5, otherwise use Fisher's test.
source_rules.correction_en: Stricter than the usual Cochran-type guidance: no expected count below 1 and at most 20% below 5. The source's own goodness-of-fit page uses that guidance, so the site is internally inconsistent.

source_rules.source_says_en: Ordinal variables are accepted.
source_rules.correction_en: The test ignores category order. With ordered categories, trend or linear-by-linear tests, or ordinal models, use that information.

source_rules.source_says_en: (implicit) Observations are cross-classified once each.
source_rules.correction_en: Paired or matched categorical data, such as before/after on the same subjects, require McNemar or Stuart-Maxwell/Bowker tests, not this test.

condition_soundness.note_en: This is the only route in the UZH tree by which two independent groups can be compared on a binary outcome. The site has no group-difference leaf for proportions (the 'proportions' leaves are one-sample tests), no McNemar leaf, and no unconditional exact test. inferguidR's explicit Boschloo endpoint therefore has no UZH counterpart; at most, the Fisher remark on this page is a related mention.

notes: Graphic colours this leaf nominal (yellow); the page accepts nominal or ordinal; the associations page says 'nominal to ordinal'.

nodes.label_en: Scale level of the dependent variable?
nodes.condition: More than two variables (several predictors, one outcome).
nodes.question_en: Is the dependent (outcome) variable interval-scaled or nominal?

condition_soundness.note_en: 'Nominal -> logistic regression' holds only for a binary outcome. Unordered outcomes with more than two categories need multinomial logistic regression, ordered outcomes ordinal (e.g. proportional-odds) regression, and counts Poisson or negative-binomial regression; ordinal outcomes are not offered at all. A binary outcome with a single predictor is also not routed to logistic regression. The 'scale levels' info link returns HTTP 404.

nodes.condition: Several predictors; interval-scaled outcome.
nodes.description_en: Models an interval outcome from several interval or dummy-coded predictors. Page covers residual diagnostics, Durbin-Watson, partial regression plots and collinearity diagnostics.
source_preconditions_en: interval outcome; predictors interval or dummy-coded

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: Tolerance should be at least 0.10 and VIF at most 10.
source_rules.correction_en: This is a common rule of thumb, not a criterion. Collinearity inflates standard errors but does not bias estimates. Whether it matters depends on the estimand: an adjusted coefficient versus prediction.

source_rules.source_says_en: Presented as cause analysis with several causes.
source_rules.correction_en: Adjusted coefficients are not causal effects without design and causal assumptions; covariate selection should follow the estimand.

source_rules.source_says_en: Simultaneous entry is recommended for theory-based models; forward, backward and stepwise selection are described as suited rather to exploratory studies.
source_rules.correction_en: Preferring pre-specified simultaneous entry is right. Stepwise selection, even in exploratory work, yields biased coefficients, invalid p-values and CIs, and unstable models; label its output as hypothesis-generating and validate it.

condition_soundness.note_en: Appropriate for interval outcomes with independent observations. Clustered or repeated outcomes need mixed or GEE models, which the tree does not cover.

nodes.condition: Several predictors; outcome nominal (assistant) or binary 0/1 (page).
nodes.description_en: Models the probability of a binary outcome from metric or dummy-coded predictors by maximum likelihood, interpreted via odds ratios, with pseudo-R2 as fit measures.
nodes.description_de: Binäre AV, mehrere UV; Interpretation über Odds Ratios.
source_preconditions_en: n >= 25 in every group formed by categorical predictors

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: The assistant routes any nominal outcome here.
source_rules.correction_en: Binary logistic regression handles two categories only. Use multinomial logistic regression for more than two unordered categories and ordinal regression for ordered ones.

source_rules.source_says_en: At least 25 cases per group formed by categorical predictors.
source_rules.correction_en: Adequacy depends on the number of events relative to model parameters, outcome prevalence and the aim (explanation versus prediction). Use events-per-parameter considerations or formal sample-size criteria for prediction models instead of a fixed per-cell n.

source_rules.source_says_en: The odds ratio is described as the change in the 'relative probability' of y = 1 per unit increase.
source_rules.correction_en: An odds ratio multiplies the odds p/(1-p), not the probability. It is non-collapsible, so adjusted and unadjusted ORs differ even without confounding. Report marginal risks or risk differences when probabilities are the estimand.

source_rules.source_says_en: Simultaneous entry and several forward/backward stepwise selection procedures (score, likelihood-ratio, Wald) are described as software options for entering predictors.
source_rules.correction_en: After data-driven stepwise selection, coefficients are biased away from zero, p-values and CIs are invalid, and the selected model is unstable. Pre-specify the model from the estimand and subject knowledge, or use penalised methods with honest validation for prediction.

condition_soundness.note_en: Correct for binary outcomes; routing by 'nominal' over-generalises (see uzh.q.assoc.multi.dv_scale).

nodes.condition: The question concerns differences (between groups or between repeated measurements).
nodes.description_en: Groups procedures for differences in central tendency/means, in variances, and in proportions/frequencies; within each group, procedures are distinguished by their preconditions.
nodes.description_de: Unterschiede in zentraler Tendenz, Varianzen und Häufigkeiten.

source_rules.source_says_en: The page says the binomial and chi-square tests examine differences in proportions or frequencies between groups.
source_rules.correction_en: Both leaves under 'proportions' are one-sample goodness-of-fit tests against a hypothesised distribution. Comparing proportions between independent groups (chi-square, Fisher, Boschloo) or between paired measurements (McNemar) is not represented in this branch.

nodes.condition: Next decision within differences.
nodes.question_en: Is interest in differences of the mean/central tendency between two or more groups, in how a variable is spread (stated by the source as how it 'is distributed') between two groups, or in whether category frequencies match expectation?

condition_soundness.note_en: Option 2 describes variance comparison as comparing how a variable is distributed between two groups, which conflates spread with distributional shape; one of its two leaves, the chi-square variance test, is a one-sample test rather than a two-group comparison. Option 3 (frequencies as expected) leads only to one-sample goodness-of-fit tests.

nodes.condition: Differences in mean or central tendency of one outcome between groups or measurements.
nodes.description_en: Ten procedures, split first by independent versus related samples, then by number of groups or measurements and grouping variables, then by distributional and scale preconditions. Mentions factorial ANOVA, or factorial repeated-measures ANOVA, for controlling a third variable.

source_rules.source_says_en: The whole branch is framed as investigating mean differences, including the rank-based tests.
source_rules.correction_en: Rank tests (Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis, Wilcoxon, Friedman) do not test means, and test medians only under strong shape assumptions. Each leaf needs an explicit estimand.

source_rules.source_says_en: To control for the effect of a third variable, a factorial ANOVA, with or without repeated measures, is suggested.
source_rules.correction_en: This works for categorical third variables. Continuous covariates call for ANCOVA or regression, and adjustment must follow the estimand.

notes: Mentioned without a leaf: factorial repeated-measures ANOVA ('mehrfaktorielle Varianzanalyse mit Messwiederholung').

nodes.label_en: Independent groups or the same group measured repeatedly?
nodes.condition: Next decision within central tendency.
nodes.question_en: Are different groups compared (independent samples), or is the same group measured more than once (related samples)?

condition_soundness.note_en: The core design question is right. Related samples also include matched pairs, twins and couples, as the page notes. Pairing must be confirmed through an explicit subject or pair ID, and clustered designs (several subjects per cluster) are not covered.

nodes.condition: Independent groups.
nodes.question_en: Two groups defined by one grouping variable, more than two groups defined by one grouping variable, or groups defined by more than one grouping variable?
nodes.question_de: 2 Gruppen, mehr als 2 Gruppen oder mehr als 1 Gruppierungsvariable?

condition_soundness.note_en: Appropriate design question. Note that the overview graphic labels the third option '1 AV, > 2 UVs', but the page text and the assistant say 'more than one'.

nodes.condition: Two independent groups, one grouping variable.
nodes.question_en: Are the variables to be treated as normally distributed or as 'distribution-free'?

condition_soundness.note_en: Asks whether 'the variables' are 'distribution-free' or 'normally distributed'. 'Distribution-free' is a property of a test, not of data. The relevant normality condition is on within-group residuals, or on paired differences for paired designs, not on raw variables. Normality pre-tests should not gate the choice. With moderate n, t-tests and ANOVA are robust to non-normality (the leaf pages themselves say violations are unproblematic above roughly 25-30 per group). Switching to a rank test changes the hypothesis tested. The 'distribution type' info link points to the descriptive page, which recommends a chi-square normality pre-test.

nodes.condition: Two independent groups; interval outcome treated as normally distributed.
method_names: Welch t-test (reported by source when Levene's test is significant)
Levene test (used by source as pre-test)
nodes.description_en: Tests whether the means of two independent groups differ. The page computes the pooled-variance statistic, checks variance homogeneity with Levene's test, reports the Welch-corrected row when variances differ, and gives r as an effect size.
source_preconditions_en: one independent variable defines the two groups

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: Levene's test decides between pooled and Welch: a non-significant result is read as showing homogeneous variances, so the pooled t-test is reported; a significant result means the Welch-corrected test is reported.
source_rules.correction_en: Non-significance does not show equal variances, and the two-stage procedure distorts the type I error rate. Use Welch's test by default; it loses little when variances are equal and protects when they and the group sizes differ. Keep Welch and pooled t as explicitly distinct variants, both for analysis and for power planning.

source_rules.source_says_en: The outcome must be normal in both populations.
source_rules.correction_en: This matters mainly for small samples, given the CLT and robustness with similar group sizes. It should be judged from design, sample size and residual diagnostics rather than a pre-test.

source_rules.source_says_en: The effect size is the correlation r derived from t, judged against Cohen's .10/.30/.50.
source_rules.correction_en: Report a standardised mean difference (d or Hedges' g, stating the standardiser) with a confidence interval, or the raw mean difference. Generic benchmarks are context-dependent.

condition_soundness.note_en: Routing via a 'distribution-free vs normal' question, and the in-page Levene gate, are both pre-test switches; see uzh.q.ct.ind.2.distribution.

nodes.condition: Two independent groups; outcome 'distribution-free' (at least ordinal).
method_names: Mann-Whitney U / Wilcoxon rank-sum test (exact or asymptotic)
nodes.description_en: Rank-based comparison of two independent groups, presented as the non-parametric counterpart of the t-test for when its preconditions fail. Medians are reported, and an exact p is used for small samples (n1 + n2 <= 30).
source_preconditions_en: one independent variable defines the two groups

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: The test is said to check whether the central tendencies (reported as medians) of two groups differ.
source_rules.correction_en: The WMW test addresses stochastic equality, P(X > Y) = P(Y > X). It is a test of medians or location only under a location-shift model with identical shapes. Report a matching estimand: probability of superiority, or a Hodges-Lehmann shift with CI under the shift assumption.

source_rules.source_says_en: Used when the t-test's preconditions are not met.
source_rules.correction_en: This is not a drop-in replacement: unequal variances also affect WMW. For means under heteroscedasticity, Welch's t is often preferable. Choose by estimand.

source_rules.source_says_en: Asymptotic p if n1 + n2 > 30, otherwise exact p.
source_rules.correction_en: The threshold is a convention. With ties, use an exact conditional or permutation p-value.

condition_soundness.note_en: See uzh.q.ct.ind.2.distribution. Ordinal outcomes are appropriately routed here, but the estimand must be stated.

nodes.label_en: Normal or 'distribution-free' (more than two independent groups)?
nodes.condition: More than two independent groups, one grouping variable.
nodes.question_en: Are the variables to be treated as normally distributed or as 'distribution-free'?

condition_soundness.note_en: Asks whether 'the variables' are 'distribution-free' or 'normally distributed'. 'Distribution-free' is a property of a test, not of data. The relevant normality condition is on within-group residuals, or on paired differences for paired designs, not on raw variables. Normality pre-tests should not gate the choice. With moderate n, t-tests and ANOVA are robust to non-normality (the leaf pages themselves say violations are unproblematic above roughly 25-30 per group). Switching to a rank test changes the hypothesis tested. The 'distribution type' info link points to the descriptive page, which recommends a chi-square normality pre-test.

nodes.condition: More than two independent groups; interval outcome treated as normal.
method_names: Welch / Brown-Forsythe ANOVA (named by source as alternatives)
nodes.description_en: Tests whether means of several independent groups defined by one categorical factor differ, followed by Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons; partial eta squared is converted to Cohen's f.
source_preconditions_en: outcome normal within each group (violations usually unproblematic above 25 per group)

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: Non-significant Levene means homogeneous variances; if significant, the classical ANOVA is said to be robust to mild violations with adequate, similar group sizes, or the Brown-Forsythe or Welch test can be used.
source_rules.correction_en: Do not gate on Levene. Welch's F is a safer default when variances or group sizes may differ.

source_rules.source_says_en: Non-normality is usually unproblematic above 25 subjects per group.
source_rules.correction_en: This is a heuristic. Robustness depends on skewness, outliers, balance and heteroscedasticity, not on n alone.

source_rules.source_says_en: Bonferroni-corrected pairwise t-tests as post-hoc tests.
source_rules.correction_en: Valid but conservative. Tukey HSD, or Games-Howell under unequal variances, are common alternatives; planned contrasts are preferable when hypotheses are specific.

condition_soundness.note_en: See uzh.q.ct.ind.k.distribution; the in-page Levene gate is a pre-test switch.

nodes.condition: More than two independent groups; outcome 'distribution-free' (at least ordinal).
method_names: Kruskal-Wallis H test (asymptotic chi-square or exact)
nodes.description_en: Rank-based comparison of several independent groups for when ANOVA preconditions fail. Gives conditions for using the chi-square approximation, otherwise an exact test, followed by Dunn-Bonferroni pairwise tests with r effect sizes.
source_preconditions_en: one independent variable defines the groups

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: The chi-square approximation is used with more than five groups, or five groups of at least 4, four groups of at least 5, or three groups of at least 9 each; otherwise an exact test.
source_rules.correction_en: This is a convention. Permutation or exact p-values are always valid alternatives.

source_rules.source_says_en: Said to test differences in central tendency.
source_rules.correction_en: It tests stochastic homogeneity across groups; medians are compared only under identical shapes.

source_rules.source_says_en: Used when ANOVA preconditions are not met.
source_rules.correction_en: Choose by estimand. Under heteroscedasticity Welch's ANOVA may answer the mean question better.

condition_soundness.note_en: See uzh.q.ct.ind.k.distribution.

nodes.condition: Independent groups defined by more than one grouping variable (factor); interval outcome.
method_names: factorial (n-way) ANOVA with main effects and interactions
nodes.description_en: Tests the main effects and interactions of several categorical factors on an interval outcome, with no stated limit on the number of factors or levels beyond adequate n. Interactions are inspected with profile plots, and Bonferroni post-hoc tests are run for factors with more than two levels.
nodes.description_de: Einfluss mehrerer kategorialer Faktoren (inkl. Interaktion) auf eine intervallskalierte AV.

path_conditions.distribution_branch: normal (graphic border only; no distribution question in the assistant)

source_preconditions_en: outcome normal within each cell (unproblematic from 25 per group)

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: If Levene's test is significant, the Brown-Forsythe or Welch test is offered as an alternative.
source_rules.correction_en: Welch and Brown-Forsythe are one-way procedures and do not apply directly to factorial main effects and interactions. For heteroscedastic factorial designs, use heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors, robust or trimmed-mean methods, or models with group-specific variances. Do not gate on Levene.

source_rules.source_says_en: (not addressed) Sums-of-squares type for unbalanced designs.
source_rules.correction_en: With unequal cell sizes, results depend on the sums-of-squares type (I/II/III) and contrast coding. The hypothesis tested must be made explicit.

condition_soundness.note_en: The overview graphic labels this branch '1 AV, > 2 UVs', which contradicts the page and assistant ('more than one'). The assistant button image for this result shows 'einfaktorielle Varianzanalyse' although it links to the factorial page; see source inconsistencies. No distribution-free alternative is offered.

nodes.condition: Same group measured repeatedly (related samples).
nodes.question_en: Is the same group measured twice or more than twice on the same variable?

condition_soundness.note_en: Appropriate. Missing measurements, unequal spacing and time-varying covariates are not considered; mixed models handle these and are absent from the tree.

nodes.condition: Two related measurements.
nodes.question_en: Are the variables to be treated as normally distributed or as 'distribution-free'?

condition_soundness.note_en: Asks whether 'the variables' are 'distribution-free' or 'normally distributed'. 'Distribution-free' is a property of a test, not of data. The relevant normality condition is on within-group residuals, or on paired differences for paired designs, not on raw variables. Normality pre-tests should not gate the choice. With moderate n, t-tests and ANOVA are robust to non-normality (the leaf pages themselves say violations are unproblematic above roughly 25-30 per group). Switching to a rank test changes the hypothesis tested. The 'distribution type' info link points to the descriptive page, which recommends a chi-square normality pre-test. For paired designs the paired-t page itself correctly states the condition for the paired differences, whereas this question asks about 'the variables'.

nodes.condition: Two related measurements; interval outcome; paired differences treated as normal.
nodes.description_en: Tests whether the mean of two related measurements differs, i.e. whether the mean paired difference is zero; r is given as an effect size.
source_preconditions_en: two related samples; pairs independent of each other
paired differences normal in the population (violations unproblematic for n > 30)

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: Normality is required for the paired differences, and is unproblematic for n > 30.
source_rules.correction_en: Correct target: the differences, not the raw variables. Pairing must be confirmed via subject ID, and incomplete pairs need an explicit missing-data decision.

source_rules.source_says_en: r as the effect size with Cohen's benchmarks.
source_rules.correction_en: Report the mean difference with CI and a clearly defined standardised effect (d_z or d_av). Generic benchmarks are context-dependent.

condition_soundness.note_en: The leaf's own condition is sound. The assistant's preceding question asks about 'variables' rather than differences.

nodes.condition: Two related measurements; 'distribution-free'.
nodes.question_en: Is the dependent variable interval-scaled or nominal?

condition_soundness.note_en: The scale-level mapping is wrong. The sign test needs at least ordinal data, since each difference must have a sign, and it is the right fallback for ordinal paired outcomes. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test ranks the sizes of the differences and so needs interval-level differences, testing symmetry about zero. Paired nominal or binary outcomes need McNemar's test (its exact form is a sign test on the discordant pairs), and Stuart-Maxwell or Bowker tests for more than two categories. The leaf pages themselves say 'at least ordinal' for both tests, so the site contradicts itself. The 'scale levels' info link returns HTTP 404.

nodes.condition: Two related measurements; 'distribution-free'; outcome interval-scaled (assistant). The page says at least ordinal.
method_names: Wilcoxon signed-rank test (exact or asymptotic z)
nodes.description_en: Rank-based comparison of two related measurements, presented as the non-parametric counterpart of the paired t-test. Uses a z-approximation for larger n, reports medians, and gives r effect sizes.
source_preconditions_en: two related samples; pairs independent of each other

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: The outcome need only be at least ordinal.
source_rules.correction_en: Ranking absolute differences requires meaningful differences, i.e. interval-level data. For purely ordinal data use the sign test. The graphic (interval fill) and the assistant (interval) are more accurate than the page here.

source_rules.source_says_en: Said to test central-tendency differences; it explains the test via the number of positive and negative differences.
source_rules.correction_en: The signed-rank test tests symmetry of the differences about zero, with the pseudo-median / Hodges-Lehmann estimate as its estimand. Counting positive versus negative differences describes the sign test.

source_rules.source_says_en: Effect size r judged against .10/.25/.40.
source_rules.correction_en: These differ from the .10/.30/.50 used on the site's other pages for the same r, so the site is internally inconsistent. Use one documented convention and prefer context.

condition_soundness.note_en: Interval-level differences without assumed normality are a legitimate reason for this test. The assistant's interval condition is acceptable; the page's 'at least ordinal' is not.

nodes.condition: Two related measurements; 'distribution-free'; outcome nominal (assistant). The page says at least ordinal.
method_names: sign test for paired data (exact binomial or asymptotic)
nodes.description_en: Compares two related measurements using only the direction of each paired difference. Zero differences (ties) need special handling; an exact p is used for fewer than 26 pairs.
nodes.description_de: Vergleich verbundener Messungen anhand der Vorzeichen der Differenzen.

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: The assistant routes nominal paired outcomes to the sign test.
source_rules.correction_en: A difference has no sign on a nominal scale. Use McNemar for paired binary outcomes and Stuart-Maxwell or Bowker for more than two categories. The page and graphic say ordinal, which is correct, so the assistant contradicts its own leaf page.

source_rules.source_says_en: Ties (zero differences) require an adjusted calculation; exact p below 26 pairs.
source_rules.correction_en: Usual practice drops zero differences, which must be reported. Exact binomial p-values are available at any n.

condition_soundness.note_en: Reached via the incorrect 'nominal' condition; the correct entry condition is an ordinal (or interval, non-symmetric) paired outcome.

nodes.label_en: Normal or 'distribution-free' (more than two related measurements)?
nodes.condition: More than two related measurements.
nodes.question_en: Are the variables to be treated as normally distributed or as 'distribution-free'?

condition_soundness.note_en: Asks whether 'the variables' are 'distribution-free' or 'normally distributed'. 'Distribution-free' is a property of a test, not of data. The relevant normality condition is on within-group residuals, or on paired differences for paired designs, not on raw variables. Normality pre-tests should not gate the choice. With moderate n, t-tests and ANOVA are robust to non-normality (the leaf pages themselves say violations are unproblematic above roughly 25-30 per group). Switching to a rank test changes the hypothesis tested. The 'distribution type' info link points to the descriptive page, which recommends a chi-square normality pre-test.

nodes.condition: More than two related measurements; interval outcome treated as normal.
nodes.description_en: Tests whether means differ across more than two related measurements. Sphericity is checked with Mauchly's test and degrees of freedom corrected by epsilon when violated, followed by Bonferroni pairwise comparisons and Cohen's f.
nodes.description_de: Mittelwertvergleich über mehr als zwei Messzeitpunkte.
source_preconditions_en: outcome normal at each time point (usually unproblematic above 25 per time point)

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: A non-significant Mauchly test means sphericity can be assumed; if it is significant, degrees of freedom are corrected.
source_rules.correction_en: Mauchly's test has low power in small samples and is sensitive to non-normality, and non-significance does not establish sphericity. Apply an epsilon correction routinely, or use the multivariate approach or a linear mixed model, which also uses incomplete cases.

source_rules.source_says_en: Greenhouse-Geisser if epsilon(GG) < .75, otherwise Huynh-Feldt.
source_rules.correction_en: A widely cited convention attributed to Girden (1992), not a theorem. Document it as a convention.

source_rules.source_says_en: The precondition is introduced as 'compound symmetry' and then tested as sphericity.
source_rules.correction_en: Compound symmetry is sufficient but not necessary for sphericity; the F-test requires sphericity.

condition_soundness.note_en: See uzh.q.ct.dep.k.distribution; the in-page Mauchly gate is a pre-test switch.

nodes.condition: More than two related measurements; outcome 'distribution-free' (at least ordinal).
nodes.description_en: Rank-based comparison of more than two related measurements, presented as the non-parametric counterpart of repeated-measures ANOVA, followed by Dunn-Bonferroni pairwise tests with r effect sizes.
source_preconditions_en: related samples; blocks (e.g. families or subjects) independent of each other

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: Used when RM-ANOVA preconditions are not met.
source_rules.correction_en: It tests whether within-block rankings differ, a different estimand from the mean, and it uses only within-block order. Choose by estimand; mixed models or aligned-rank methods are alternatives.

source_rules.source_says_en: Dunn-Bonferroni post-hoc tests on mean ranks.
source_rules.correction_en: Mean-rank pairwise comparisons depend on the other groups in the design. Pairwise Wilcoxon or sign tests with multiplicity adjustment are an alternative.

condition_soundness.note_en: See uzh.q.ct.dep.k.distribution.

nodes.condition: Interest in differences of spread (variance).
nodes.description_en: Two tests of variance differences, distinguished by preconditions: a chi-square test comparing a sample variance with a population variance, and the F-test comparing variances between groups. Levene's test is deferred to the ANOVA pages.

source_rules.source_says_en: The chi-square test is said to compare variances of variables of any scale level.
source_rules.correction_en: A variance is defined only for interval or ratio data. The chi-square variance leaf page itself requires interval data and normality, so the site contradicts itself.

nodes.condition: Next decision within variances.
nodes.question_en: Are the variables to be treated as 'distribution-free' or as normally distributed?

condition_soundness.note_en: The assistant sends 'distribution-free' data to the chi-square variance test, which its own leaf page describes as requiring normality, being non-robust and needing a known population variance. The overview graphic marks neither variance test with a normal or distribution-free border. Distribution-robust comparisons of spread between groups (Brown-Forsythe/median-Levene, Fligner-Killeen, bootstrap) are not offered.

nodes.label_en: Chi-square test for a single variance
nodes.condition: Variances; 'distribution-free' (as stated by the assistant).
method_names: one-sample chi-square test of a variance against a known population variance
nodes.description_en: Tests whether the variance observed in one sample equals a known population variance.
source_preconditions_en: trait normal in the population (test not robust)

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: The assistant reaches this test via 'distribution-free'.
source_rules.correction_en: The test is exact only under normality and is notoriously non-robust; the leaf page states this.

source_rules.source_says_en: Offered as a way to examine variance differences (between groups, per the assistant's question).
source_rules.correction_en: This is a one-sample test against a known sigma-squared. It cannot compare two or more groups. Use Brown-Forsythe, Fligner-Killeen or bootstrap methods for robust between-group comparison of spread.

condition_soundness.note_en: Both the 'distribution-free' routing and the framing as a group comparison are wrong.

notes: The preconditions heading on this page is a copy-paste remnant: it names the repeated-measures ANOVA.

nodes.label_en: F-test for equality of two variances
nodes.condition: Variances; normally distributed; two independent groups.
method_names: F-test (variance ratio) for two independent samples
nodes.description_en: Tests whether two independent samples have homogeneous variances; framed as a precondition check, with Levene's test via the t-test procedure as an alternative.

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: The F/Levene test is used to check the homogeneity precondition for other tests; a non-significant result is said to confirm that the variances do not differ.
source_rules.correction_en: Non-significance is not evidence of equality, and using variance pre-tests to choose between pooled and Welch t is discouraged.

source_rules.source_says_en: Normality required.
source_rules.correction_en: The variance-ratio F-test is extremely sensitive to non-normality, so normality is essential. If a variance difference is itself the estimand, report the ratio with CI and consider robust tests.

condition_soundness.note_en: Normality is indeed required. The test's use as a pre-test is questionable.

nodes.condition: Interest in whether category frequencies match an expected distribution.
nodes.description_en: Two one-sample tests of observed frequencies against a hypothesised distribution: the binomial test for a dichotomous variable and the chi-square goodness-of-fit test for categorical variables (illustrated as a normality check).
notes: Despite sitting under 'Unterschiede', this branch contains only one-sample goodness-of-fit tests; see source rule uzh.r.diff.prop_between_groups.

nodes.label_en: Two or more than two categories?
nodes.condition: Next decision within proportions.
nodes.question_en: Does the variable have exactly two categories (response options) or more than two?

condition_soundness.note_en: A workable split, but not exclusive. The goodness-of-fit page's own worked example is a two-category 3:1 hypothesis, and the overview graphic offers both tests without this condition. Exact multinomial tests are an option for small expected counts.

nodes.condition: Dichotomous variable; observed proportion versus a hypothesised probability.
nodes.description_en: Tests whether the frequency of one of two categories matches a hypothesised probability (e.g. guessing in a multiple-choice test), reported as an exact two-sided p-value.
nodes.description_de: Anteil einer dichotomen Variable vs. erwartete Wahrscheinlichkeit.

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: Exact binomial test of one proportion against a hypothesised value.
source_rules.correction_en: Sound for one independent sample. It is not a comparison of two groups' proportions. Two-sided exact p-value definitions differ between software, so state which is used.

condition_soundness.note_en: Appropriate for a one-sample binary outcome.

nodes.condition: Categorical variable with more than two categories; observed versus hypothesised distribution.
method_names: Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of normality (as presented by source)
nodes.description_en: Compares the observed category frequencies of one variable with a theoretically expected distribution, which may be arbitrary. Special cases shown: checking normality by binning, and a Kolmogorov-Smirnov normality test.
nodes.description_de: Beobachtete vs. erwartete Häufigkeitsverteilung einer Variable.
source_preconditions_en: every expected count at least 1 and at most 20% below 5 (general case)
all expected counts at least 5 (normality case)
K-S: continuous variable; not suited to large samples

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: A common use is to check whether a variable is normally distributed (e.g. IQ before further analysis); a non-significant result is desirable when normal data are needed.
source_rules.correction_en: Non-significance does not establish normality, and normality pre-tests should not gate later method choice.

source_rules.source_says_en: The binned normality example reports Chi-Quadrat(5, n = 31) for six categories (df = k - 1), with expected counts supplied as given numbers and no statement of how the normal's mean and SD were obtained.
source_rules.correction_en: When testing a single sample for normality, mean and SD are normally estimated from that sample. The reference distribution then has about k - 1 - 2 df, and grouping ungrouped data has further subtleties. The page does not discuss this; df = k - 1 is correct only for a fully pre-specified normal.

source_rules.source_says_en: The K-S test compares the data with a normal distribution having the sample's own mean and SD.
source_rules.correction_en: With estimated parameters the standard K-S null distribution is invalid and conservative; the Lilliefors correction (or a different normality test) is required.

source_rules.source_says_en: K-S is recommended only for small samples because in large samples it 'wrongly' becomes significant although the distribution does not differ.
source_rules.correction_en: Large samples detect small but real deviations; these are not false positives, though they may be practically irrelevant. The real issue is that significance is not a measure of relevance.

source_rules.source_says_en: General case: every expected count at least 1 and at most 20% below 5. Normality case: all at least 5.
source_rules.correction_en: The Cochran-type rule is standard. The two sections of the page are inconsistent with each other and with the contingency page's 'all > 5' rule.

condition_soundness.note_en: Appropriate for a one-sample categorical distribution with fully specified expected proportions. Its use as a normality pre-test is questionable.

nodes.condition: Little prior theory; structure among many variables or many objects is to be discovered.
nodes.description_en: Structure-discovering procedures without a dependent/independent split. Factor and cluster analysis are presented, MDS and conjoint analysis are only named, and exploratory and confirmatory variants are distinguished.
notes: Mentioned without a leaf: multidimensional scaling, conjoint analysis, confirmatory factor analysis.

nodes.condition: Next decision within interdependence analysis.
nodes.question_en: Are many variables to be summarised into a few dimensions, or are many persons or objects to be grouped?

condition_soundness.note_en: Appropriate split between variable-oriented and case-oriented exploratory structure.

nodes.condition: Many variables are to be summarised into few factors.
nodes.description_en: Exploratory factor analysis summarises many variables into a few factors without prior hypotheses (Big Five given as an example).

nodes.condition: Summarise many interval (in practice often ordinal) variables into few factors; no further condition.
method_names: principal component analysis (used in the worked example)
KMO / MSA, Bartlett test of sphericity
nodes.description_en: Summarises groups of interval variables into factors. Covers suitability checks (KMO, Bartlett), extraction (PCA as the worked example, PAF named), number of factors (Kaiser criterion, scree plot, interpretability) and rotation (varimax, oblimin).
nodes.description_de: Bündelung vieler Variablen zu wenigen Faktoren.
source_preconditions_en: sample large enough (rule of thumb: at least 10 cases per variable)
enough variables (rule of thumb: 4 or more per factor)
variables interval-scaled (ordinal often used in practice)

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: PCA is used as the worked example of a factor analysis, while noting that strictly it is not one.
source_rules.correction_en: PCA and common-factor EFA (PAF, ML) answer different questions. For latent-factor interpretation, use EFA.

source_rules.source_says_en: The number of factors is guided by the Kaiser criterion (eigenvalue > 1, acknowledged as debated), the scree plot and interpretability.
source_rules.correction_en: The Kaiser rule tends to over-extract. Prefer parallel analysis or similar criteria, combined with theory and interpretability.

source_rules.source_says_en: At least 10 cases per variable.
source_rules.correction_en: Required n depends on communalities and factor over-determination more than on a fixed ratio.

source_rules.source_says_en: The Bartlett test (assumes normality) is used to show the variables are not completely uncorrelated.
source_rules.correction_en: Almost always significant at typical n, so it adds little; KMO/MSA is more informative.

source_rules.source_says_en: Ordinal variables are often used in practice.
source_rules.correction_en: For ordinal items, base EFA on polychoric correlations, or use item-factor models.

condition_soundness.note_en: Exploratory, so conventional test-based power planning is not applicable; precision or stability planning would need separate justification.

nodes.condition: Many persons/objects are to be grouped into few clusters.
nodes.description_en: Cluster analysis combines objects into a few groups on the basis of their characteristics, with the number of groups determined by the analysis rather than in advance.

nodes.condition: Group objects into natural groups; no further condition.
method_names: hierarchical agglomerative clustering (single, complete, average, centroid, median linkage; Ward method)
proximity measures: squared Euclidean, Euclidean, city-block, Minkowski
dendrogram-based choice of number of clusters
nodes.description_en: Groups objects into natural clusters. Covers proximity measures, the families of agglomerative linkage and variance methods (Ward used in the example), and choosing the number of clusters from the largest heterogeneity increase in the dendrogram.

path_conditions.scale_level: any (graphic); one common level required for the software shown

source_preconditions_en: sample large enough if inferring to a population (small samples common)
missing values handled beforehand (deletion, mean replacement or imputation)
all clustering variables on the same scale level, often by downgrading to the lowest

graphic_encoding.read_by: visual inspection of entscheidbaum.jpg (overview graphic) on 2026-10-03

source_rules.source_says_en: Mean replacement is listed as an option for missing values.
source_rules.correction_en: Mean imputation shrinks variances and distorts distances. Prefer justified complete-case analysis, multiple imputation, or distance measures that handle missingness.

source_rules.source_says_en: Mixed scale levels are often transformed down to the lowest common level.
source_rules.correction_en: This discards information. Mixed-type distances such as Gower's coefficient avoid it.

source_rules.source_says_en: The number of clusters is chosen from the largest heterogeneity increase in the dendrogram plus content considerations.
source_rules.correction_en: Also assess stability and validity (resampling, silhouette, agreement across algorithms). Algorithms return clusters even for structureless data.

condition_soundness.note_en: Exploratory; results depend on distance, standardisation and algorithm choices. No conventional power analysis applies.

edges.condition: Aim: describe distributions of single variables
Theory or concrete question about dependent vs independent variables (assistant option 1)
One variable designated as dependent (presumed direction)
Mean / central-tendency differences between two or more groups
More than two groups (one grouping variable)
Outcome nominal (as stated by the assistant)
Spread/variance differences (source: how a variable is distributed between two groups)
Frequencies of a variable as expected
Little theory; structures to be discovered (assistant option 2)

gaps.description: In the overview image map (entscheidbaum.html), the 'Dependenzanalyse' area href contains a space inside the host name ('//www.methodenberatung.uzh.ch /datenanalyse_spss/dependenz.html'), so the URL is invalid (curl: bad hostname). The target page was fetched via its CMS URL instead.

The assistant's 'scale levels' info link (/skalenniveau.html, on entscheid111, entscheid112 and entscheid121211) redirects to /de/skalenniveau.html, which returns HTTP 404. A scale-level page exists at /de/Ressourcen--Beratung/skalenniveau.html (HTTP 200, outside the transcribed scope; content not transcribed).

Two legacy CMS links are dead: http://cms.uzh.ch/lenya/.../deskuniv.html on the dependence page (host does not resolve) and /lenya/methodenberatung/datenanalyse/zusammenhaenge/rangkorrelation.html.html on the correlation page (HTTP 404). In both cases the current target page was fetched via the navigation.

Image-map and assistant hrefs use legacy paths without '/de/' (e.g. //www.methodenberatung.uzh.ch/datenanalyse_spss/unterschiede/zentral/mann.html). These answered with a 302 redirect to the '/de/' URL on 2026-10-03 (checked for mann, faktor, dependenz, deskuniv). Node source_url values use the canonical '/de/' URLs.

The overview decision tree and its sub-graphics are JPEG bitmaps with HTML image maps; no JS or JSON data exists behind them (page source inspected: no scripts). Box labels, branch labels and the colour legend (fill = scale level of the (dependent) variable; border = normal / distribution-free) were read by visual inspection. Border presence was cross-checked by sampling pixel colours. Image-map hrefs and coordinates were taken from the HTML.

Inline figures and formula images on content pages (design illustrations 'Abbildung n', SPSS output screenshots, equation images) were not opened. They illustrate examples, computations and software output, not branch conditions. The text around them was read.
22 linked SPSS example datasets (.sav under /dam/jcr:...) were not downloaded. They are software-specific and outside the R-only scope.

No English version of the section exists (/en/datenanalyse_spss.html and /en.html returned HTTP 404 on 2026-10-03). All English labels and descriptions are original translations and paraphrases; German short labels are close to the source wording.

Methods named in source text with no leaf page of their own: factorial repeated-measures ANOVA; Welch t-test, Welch ANOVA and Brown-Forsythe test (in-page alternatives); Levene test (in-page pre-test); Kolmogorov-Smirnov and chi-square normality tests (in the goodness-of-fit page); Fisher exact test and Yates correction (in the contingency page); Dunn-Bonferroni post-hoc tests; discriminant analysis (dependence page); multidimensional scaling, conjoint analysis and confirmatory factor analysis (interdependence page); multinomial/ordinal regression extensions (associations page); principal axis factoring (factor page).

Not represented anywhere in the transcribed UZH taxonomy, though relevant to inferguidR: comparison of two independent proportions as a group difference (only reachable as 2x2 contingency chi-square, with Fisher as an in-page remark); Boschloo or other unconditional exact tests; McNemar and Cochran's Q (paired binary); mixed or multilevel models and GEE (clustered or repeated data with missingness); ANCOVA; MANOVA; ordinal, multinomial and count regression; survival analysis; equivalence and non-inferiority testing; partial correlation; diagnostic or classification performance (ROC, cut-offs); study planning (power and sample size).

CMS page HTML is not byte-stable across fetches: each response carries random 'main-nav_overlay_<uuid>' ids, and four pages (correlation, rank correlation, multiple regression, logistic regression) serve figure/equation image URLs with varying timestamp suffixes. page_sha256 is the raw hash of the archived fetch used for transcription. page_sha256_nav_normalized masks the uuid ids; it was equal on re-fetch for 30/34 pages, the other 4 differing only in image-URL suffixes. main_text_sha256 (whitespace-normalised text of <main>) was equal on re-fetch for the 4 volatile pages and should be used for drift detection. Static graphics and assistant files were byte-identical on re-fetch.

The assistant routes nominal paired outcomes to the sign test and interval ones to the Wilcoxon test. The sign-test page says 'at least ordinal' and the graphic colours it ordinal; the Wilcoxon page says 'at least ordinal' while the graphic colours it interval.

source_inconsistencies.description: The assistant routes 'distribution-free' to the chi-square variance test; that test's page requires normality, calls it non-robust and requires a known population variance; the variances page says it works for any scale level; the graphic marks neither variance test with a distribution border.
source_inconsistencies.evidence: assistant text; leaf preconditions; variances page; graphic

source_inconsistencies.description: The preconditions heading on the chi-square variance page names the one-way repeated-measures ANOVA (copy-paste remnant).
The differences page says the proportion tests compare groups; both proportion leaves are one-sample goodness-of-fit tests.
Expected-count rules differ across the site: contingency page 'all > 5'; goodness-of-fit page 'all >= 1 and at most 20% < 5' (general case) and 'all >= 5' (normality case).
The Wilcoxon page benchmarks r as .10/.25/.40, while the other pages use .10/.30/.50 for the same r.
The assistant offers logistic regression for a 'nominal' outcome; the logistic page and the associations page restrict it to binary outcomes.
Minor ALT-text typos on assistant buttons: 'Mann-Withney U', 'Binominaltest', 'Wilkoxon Test' (the last two also appear in the button images and page URL slugs).
